absolute value: The distance of a number from zero on the number line, always nonnegative.
absolute value equation: An equation of the form |ax+b|=c, solved by setting the inside equal to both c and -c.
absolute value inequality — conjunction: An inequality like |ax+b|<c, rewritten as the compound range -c<ax+b<c.
absolute value inequality — disjunction: An inequality like |ax+b|>c, split into ax+b>c or ax+b<-c.
boundary line: The line drawn from an inequality's equality part; solid if endpoints are included, dashed if not.
composite function: A function (f∘g)(x)=f(g(x)) formed by applying one function to the output of another.
domain: The set of all input values (x) for which a function is defined.
elimination method: Solving a system by adding or subtracting equations to cancel one variable.
feasible region: The region of points satisfying all inequalities in a system, used in linear programming.
function: A relation assigning exactly one output to each input value.
function notation: Writing y=f(x) to denote the output of function f for a given input x.
horizontal shift: A transformation y=f(x-h) that moves a graph right (h>0) or left (h<0).
infinite solutions — 부정: When two equations describe the same line, giving infinitely many shared solutions.
interval notation: A way to write solution sets using parentheses for excluded and brackets for included endpoints.
linear equation: An equation whose variable has degree one, having a single numerical solution.
linear inequality: A degree-one statement using <, >, ≤, or ≥; reversing the sign when multiplying by a negative.
no solution — 불능: When two equations describe parallel lines, yielding a false statement and no solution.
range: The set of all output values (y) a function produces over its domain.
relation: Any set of ordered pairs linking inputs to outputs, not necessarily a function.
solution set: The set of all values that make an equation or inequality true.
substitution method: Solving a system by replacing one variable with an expression from another equation.
system of inequalities: Two or more inequalities whose common solution region is their intersection.
test point: A point not on the boundary line plugged into an inequality to determine the solution side.
vertical stretch/compression: A transformation y=a·f(x) that stretches (|a|>1) or compresses (|a|<1) a graph vertically.
addition/subtraction: Combining complex numbers by adding or subtracting their real and imaginary parts separately.
completing the square: Rewriting a quadratic as a perfect square plus a constant to solve it or find the vertex.
complex conjugate: The number a-bi paired with a+bi; their product a²+b² is always real.
complex number: A number of the form a+bi, with a the real part and b the imaginary part.
conjugate pair of solutions: Imaginary roots of a real-coefficient quadratic always occur as conjugates a+bi and a-bi.
discriminant: The expression b²-4ac that reveals the number and type of a quadratic's roots.
division of complex numbers: Dividing complex numbers by multiplying numerator and denominator by the denominator's conjugate.
factored form: A quadratic written y=a(x-p)(x-q), showing its x-intercepts p and q directly.
factoring: Rewriting a polynomial as a product of simpler factors.
gcf — greatest common factor: The largest factor common to all terms, factored out first when factoring.
imaginary unit: The number i defined by i²=-1, the square root of negative one.
imaginary/complex solution: A solution that is not real, arising when the discriminant is negative.
multiplication: Multiplying complex numbers by FOIL expansion and replacing i² with -1.
parabola: The U-shaped graph of a quadratic function, symmetric about its axis.
perfect square trinomial: A trinomial of the form x²+2nx+n² that factors as (x+n)².
quadratic formula: The formula x=(-b±√(b²-4ac))/(2a) giving the solutions of any quadratic.
square root method: Solving (x-h)²=k by taking the square root of both sides to get x=h±√k.
standard form: A quadratic written y=ax²+bx+c, from which the y-intercept c is read directly.
symmetry: The property that a parabola mirrors itself across its axis of symmetry.
vertex form: A quadratic written y=a(x-h)²+k, showing its vertex (h,k) directly.
vieta's formulas: Relations giving a quadratic's root sum as -b/a and root product as c/a.
x-intercept / zero: The x-value where a graph crosses the x-axis, found by setting y=0.
y-intercept: The point where a graph crosses the y-axis, found by setting x=0.
zero product property: If a product AB=0, then A=0 or B=0, enabling solving by factoring.
continuity & ivt: Polynomials are continuous; the Intermediate Value Theorem guarantees a root between sign changes.
division algorithm: The relation f(x)=d(x)q(x)+r(x), where the remainder's degree is below the divisor's.
end behavior: How a function's values behave as x approaches positive or negative infinity, set by the leading term.
factor theorem: A polynomial f has factor (x-c) if and only if f(c)=0.
full factoring routine: A systematic process using rational roots, the factor theorem, and division to factor fully.
gcf factoring: Pulling out the greatest common factor as the first step of factoring.
grouping: Factoring four or more terms in pairs to extract a common binomial factor.
leading term: The term of highest degree in a polynomial, determining its degree and end behavior.
local maximum / local minimum: A point where a graph reaches a peak or valley relative to nearby points.
missing terms: Placeholder zero coefficients written for absent powers when dividing polynomials.
multiplicity: The number of times a factor repeats, determining whether a graph crosses or touches the x-axis.
perfect cube: A number or expression that is the cube of another, such as 8 or x³.
polynomial: An expression made of summed terms with whole-number variable exponents.
polynomial long division: Dividing one polynomial by another using a process like numerical long division.
quadratic form substitution: Substituting u=x² to turn an equation like ax⁴+bx²+c into a quadratic in u.
rational root theorem: Possible rational roots are ±p/q, with p dividing the constant and q the leading coefficient.
remainder theorem: The remainder of dividing f(x) by (x-c) equals f(c).
soap mnemonic: A memory aid (Same, Opposite, Always Positive) for the signs in cube factoring formulas.
synthetic division: A shortcut for dividing a polynomial by a linear factor (x-c) using only coefficients.
writing equations from graphs: Building a polynomial's equation from its x-intercepts, multiplicities, and a known point.
zero / real root: An x-value where f(x)=0, where the graph meets the x-axis.
adding & subtracting rational expression: Combining rational expressions over a common denominator, then simplifying the result.
basic radical function: A function such as f(x)=√x, the starting parent graph for radical transformations.
checking for extraneous solutions: Substituting solutions back into the original equation to discard ones introduced by squaring.
domain & range: The allowed input values and resulting output values of a radical function.
domain restrictions: Excluded input values, such as those making a denominator zero.
extraneous solution: An apparent solution that fails in the original equation and must be discarded.
hole / removable discontinuity: A single missing point where a common factor cancels from a rational function.
horizontal asymptote: A horizontal line that a graph approaches as x goes to positive or negative infinity.
inverse relationship: The way f(x)=x² (x≥0) and g(x)=√x undo each other as inverse functions.
isolating the radical: Moving a radical term alone to one side before raising both sides to a power.
laws of exponents: Rules for combining powers that also apply to rational exponents.
lcd: least common denominator: The smallest expression divisible by all denominators, used to combine fractions.
multiplication & division: Multiplying or dividing rational expressions by canceling factors, dividing by the reciprocal.
nth root: A value a where aⁿ=b, written ⁿ√b.
nth-root equations: Equations with cube, fourth, or higher roots, solved by raising both sides to that power.
radical equation: An equation with a variable inside a radical, solved by isolating and raising to a power.
rational equation: An equation containing fractions, solved by multiplying through by the LCD.
rational exponent: A fractional exponent x^(m/n) equal to the nth root of x to the m power.
rational expression: A fraction whose numerator and denominator are both polynomials.
rationalizing the denominator: Removing a radical from a denominator by multiplying by a suitable factor or conjugate.
simplifying rational expressions: Reducing a rational expression by factoring and canceling common factors.
transformations of radical functions: Shifting, stretching, or reflecting a radical's parent graph using parameters a, h, and k.
transformations of rational functions: Shifting, stretching, or reflecting f(x)=1/x using parameters that set its asymptotes.
vertical asymptote: A vertical line x=a that a graph approaches but never reaches, where the denominator is zero.
